docs.text: Morse ... --- ... sent as one signal, not three separate letters with word gaps. Source: ITU Morse; COLREGS Annex IV.
MAYDAY is grave and imminent danger, said three times. PAN-PAN is urgency, not yet distress. Spoken on the radio, then who you are, where you are, what you need. Source: ITU radio procedure.
Stand facing the searcher. Slowly and repeatedly raise and lower both arms outstretched to each side. Source: COLREGS Annex IV — distress signals.

Three gunshots about a minute apart, three whistle blasts, three fires in a triangle, or three grouped mirror flashes. Answer is often one long and one short, or the same pattern repeated. Source: COLREGS Annex IV; common SAR practice.
Orange smoke, an orange panel, or a dye marker is a seen distress mark. A square flag with a ball above or below it is also a distress signal. Source: COLREGS Annex IV.
Require assistance. Source: FAA AIM 6-2-6 survivor ground-air code.
Require medical assistance. Source: FAA AIM 6-2-6 survivor ground-air code.
No. Negative. Source: FAA AIM 6-2-6 survivor ground-air code.
Yes. Affirmative. Source: FAA AIM 6-2-6 survivor ground-air code.
Proceeding in this direction. Point the arrow the way you are moving. Source: FAA AIM 6-2-6 survivor ground-air code.

One aimed flash to get attention. Do not flash continuously into a cockpit. Three grouped flashes is the distress pattern if they have not seen you. Source: SAR practice; three-of-anything distress pattern.
Three blasts, pause, three blasts. A whistle carries farther than a voice in wind and timber. Source: COLREGS three-sound distress pattern.
